content: The cost per diagnostic test decreases as the utilization of testing services increases. This cost reduction is achieved by distributing expenses across various activities and programs, including the procurement and maintenance of diagnostic instruments, logistics, supply chain management, human resources, sample transportation, training and mentoring, waste management, data management, quality assurance, and the delivery of test results. Sharing these costs among different programs can lead to overall cost savings and more efficient resource utilization. Costs can be allocated between host and beneficiary programs using different strategies, such as by testing volumes, assigning entire cost items to specific programs, or accounting for prior investments. Significant cost savings are primarily achieved by sharing the expenses of diagnostic devices and their maintenance. Utilizing existing diagnostic device fleets with available capacity is a practical and cost-effective approach to expanding access to testing services. Tools are available to help countries understand potential cost savings and identify the most efficient and effective strategies for diagnostic integration. A systematic review conducted up to June 2020 identified two observational studies that evaluated the outcomes of integrating HIV and tuberculosis (TB) testing. One study was conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Zimbabwe, and the other by the Clinton Health Access Initiative in Malawi and Zimbabwe. These studies examined the impact of integrating HIV testing with TB testing and its effects on TB testing volumes and the programs responsible for procuring and implementing the diagnostic technology. Even after integrating HIV infant diagnosis and targeted HIV viral load testing, TB testing accounted for approximately 60% of the total testing volume. Despite the increase in overall testing volumes, device utilization never exceeded 75% of capacity. Importantly, no adverse effects were observed on the turnaround time for test results or on TB treatment initiation rates following the integration of HIV testing. In fact, the addition of HIV infant diagnosis and targeted viral load testing resulted in faster turnaround times, higher treatment initiation rates, and improved clinical outcomes for infants living with HIV and individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) experiencing viremia. Offering integrated testing for TB, HIV infant diagnosis, and targeted HIV viral load testing increased device utilization without exceeding capacity or negatively impacting TB services. These findings demonstrate that integrated testing is operationally feasible when appropriate site selection is used to balance expected demand. TB testing and treatment services continued to be provided at the same rate as before integration. The Guideline Development Group, based on available evidence and country experiences, recommended integrating diagnostic services across disease programs as a good practice. This integration is expected to result in net overall benefits, including increased efficiency, more comprehensive care for people living with HIV, and optimized diagnostic networks. Sharing diagnostic devices and operational costs can enable more integrated health services and improve access to testing by expanding the device base and leveraging program knowledge. Diagnostic integration is also anticipated to create a more robust and responsive diagnostic network, better equipped to address outbreaks and pandemics. However, knowledge gaps remain, and further research is needed to measure the impact of diagnostic integration across various diseases, including HIV, TB, hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections, cervical cancer, and disease outbreaks. Implementation research is also necessary to establish best practices for diagnostic integration and sustainable quality assurance approaches within broader, integrated networks. Updated guidelines on service delivery for the treatment and care of people living with HIV will be made available on the WHO HIV website. Key findings and recommendations will be disseminated through policy briefs, printed materials, PDFs, social media links, and the WHO HIV Tx App, a free mobile application for easy access and reference. Translations into other official languages will be developed in collaboration with regional and country offices. The Department of Global HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes will monitor the uptake of HIV-related recommendations through mechanisms such as the Global AIDS Monitoring framework, country surveys, and population-based HIV impact assessments. These efforts will provide indirect evidence of the impact of WHO recommendations. The department will also work with regional and country offices, donors, and implementing partners to support the adoption and implementation of these guidelines. Potential barriers to implementation include delays in dissemination due to the time required for translation and limited resources in some countries to update existing policies. Ongoing scoping reviews will anticipate future guidance needs, and rapid technical updates will complement guideline updates when necessary.
